Okay here's a pattern I keep running into and I want to know if there's a cleaner way to write it. I've got a handful of functions that each return a promise, one hits an endpoint for user data, another fetches their recent orders, a third grabs their preferences, and right now I'm chaining them with a bunch of nested `.then()` calls where each one waits on the last before firing the next, even though none of them actually depend on each other's results. It works, but it reads like a staircase and it's slower than it needs to be since they run one after another instead of at the same time. I've seen people wrap a batch of promises together and await the whole group at once so everything kicks off in parallel and you just get all the results back together at the end, but I've also seen warnings that if any single one of those rejects, the whole group blows up immediately even if the others would've succeeded fine. Is there a version of that same idea that waits for every promise to settle, success or failure, and gives you a status for each one individually, so I can handle partial failures gracefully instead of one bad request torpedoing the whole batch? In my working years I was something of a stickler for tidiness, and that habit has followed me into this new hobby of mine rather more than I expected. I have been building a small image for a personal project, and my first attempt was, in retrospect, rather sloppy: a single build file that installed every compiler and development tool needed to produce the application, then simply shipped that same bloated result to run in production, weighing in at well over a gigabyte for what amounts to a modest little program. A younger colleague of my son's, who was kind enough to look over my shoulder one afternoon, suggested I split the build file into two stages instead: one stage with all the heavy compilation tools that produces the finished binary, and a second, much leaner stage that copies only that finished binary out of the first and discards everything else, bringing the final size down to a small fraction of what it was. He also mentioned, almost in passing, that I ought to order my instructions so that anything unlikely to change, such as installing dependencies, happens before I copy in my own source files, since apparently the build process can then reuse earlier work instead of redoing it from scratch every time I make the smallest edit to my code. Lastly, he suggested running the finished program as an ordinary unprivileged user inside the image rather than as the default administrative one, which he assured me is simply considered good manners these days rather than an eccentric precaution. I have made all three changes and the difference, both in size and in the time it takes to rebuild after a small change, has been rather remarkable
